rationale: A wins because it keeps the story anchored to provable newsroom shapes instead of inflating the rollout into a market trend. A's "Khan Academy says its AI tutor added weeks of learning. Its own study is the first test of that claim" pairs the headline claim with the methodological trap. B opens with "30 districts signing on simultaneously is a measurable data point on how fast AI tutoring is moving into public schools," which is a bigger claim than the update earns. Competent work, but that is a product announcement wearing a trend-story costume.
gaps_in_A: "Donors, not districts, are paying" overstates the supplied fact. The update says donor-funded and free to teachers; A later asks the right question about whether districts pay, but the headline gets ahead of the evidence.

"The district is joining the rollout, or its pilot results are part of what is being published now" is conditional and partly speculative. The local angle is useful only after Khan names a real district willing to talk.

"Founder profile of Khan Academy's leadership" is correctly refused, but the set misses a cleaner teacher-workflow angle around lesson planning because it lacks proof of actual teacher adoption or time saved.
gaps_in_B: "30 districts signing on simultaneously" invents simultaneity. The update says Khan is rolling out to 30 more districts; it does not say they signed at once or prove an adoption pattern.
"how fast AI tutoring is moving into public schools" turns one Khan rollout into a sector trend without a baseline. That is exactly the sort of fake peg a reporter will punish.
"Donors, not school districts, are footing the bill" is too firm. The update supports donor funding and free access for teachers, not necessarily free district or student access.

"Inside one pilot district's Khanmigo classrooms" is refused as hallucinated, but that is too blunt. It should be held as a conditional local angle once a named district, teacher, and district-level result exist.
